name: Falsetto-Nimbus
geological_features: Unusually high-altitude cloud decks reaching extreme altitudes
Narrow atmospheric bands in pastel shades
A small but dense core of metallic elements
specific_features: The High Voice — atmospheric resonance that produces radio emissions at unusually high frequencies
Iridescent cloud layers that shimmer in pearl and opal tones
resources: Ammonia ice crystals for industrial chemistry
description: Falsetto-Nimbus is a medium-sized gas giant distinguished by its unusually high-pitched radio emissions and its delicate, pastel-colored atmosphere. Where most gas giants display bold, saturated bands, Falsetto-Nimbus is painted in soft pearl, lavender, rose, and cream — the result of high-altitude ammonia ice crystals that scatter light differently than the deeper cloud decks of larger worlds.

The planet emits radio noise at frequencies far above the norm for gas giants, a phenomenon attributed to unusual electromagnetic conditions in its upper atmosphere. The emissions have a quality that, when converted to audible frequencies, sounds eerily like a human falsetto — a coincidence that gave the planet its name. The effect is unsettling to crews who monitor communications in the planet's vicinity.

Falsetto-Nimbus occupies an unusual orbital position, shepherding a ring of captured asteroids and ice fragments that form a broad, diffuse disc around the planet. The ring material is slowly spiraling inward, and atmospheric models predict it will begin impacting the upper atmosphere within a few centuries, potentially altering the planet's coloration and radio characteristics permanently.

The planet's primary value is as a fuel depot — its hydrogen reserves are easily accessible due to the relatively calm upper atmosphere, and its position along a major trade route makes it a convenient stopping point. A network of orbital stations and fuel processing facilities has grown up around it, creating one of the busiest deep-space industrial complexes in the region. The impending ring collapse is a concern, as the debris could threaten orbital infrastructure.
